clinicalPearls: A severe transfusion reaction, most often seen in sickle cell disease and thalassaemia, in which both transfused and the patient's own red cells are destroyed.
The hallmark is a post-transfusion haemoglobin that falls below the pre-transfusion level, so the patient is worse off after being transfused.
Markedly raised lactate dehydrogenase, low haptoglobin, haemoglobinuria and often a reticulocytopenia despite severe anaemia are characteristic.
Acute and delayed forms are described; the delayed form frequently coincides with an alloantibody response while the acute form may occur without detectable new antibodies.
Further transfusion typically worsens haemolysis and should be avoided unless anaemia is immediately life-threatening.
Immunosuppression with corticosteroids and immunoglobulin is the mainstay, with complement inhibition and other agents considered in refractory cases.
In sickle cell disease it may be mistaken for a painful crisis, delaying recognition and prompting harmful further transfusion.
Bystander destruction of autologous cells is thought to involve activated macrophages and complement, extending haemolysis beyond antigen-incompatible cells.
reference.pathophysiology: Hyperhaemolysis syndrome is characterised by destruction of red cells in excess of the transfused incompatible units, so that autologous cells are also lost. The mechanism is incompletely understood but is thought to involve intense macrophage activation and complement dysregulation triggered by transfusion in a chronically alloimmunised and inflamed host. Activated macrophages destroy both antibody-coated transfused cells and innocent bystander autologous red cells, while suppression of erythropoiesis (a relative reticulocytopenia) compounds the fall in haemoglobin. In the delayed form an anamnestic alloantibody response is often demonstrable, whereas the acute form may occur without new detectable antibodies, suggesting antibody-independent mechanisms. The result is profound, worsening anaemia with brisk intravascular and extravascular haemolysis.
additionalDifferentials: Sickle cell vaso-occlusive crisis with anaemia
additionalInvestigations: Serial haemoglobin demonstrating a fall below the pre-transfusion value
Lactate dehydrogenase, bilirubin and haptoglobin confirming brisk haemolysis
Reticulocyte count, which may be inappropriately low
Direct antiglobulin test and extended antibody identification
Review of transfusion history and haemoglobin electrophoresis to quantify remaining donor haemoglobin
redFlags: Post-transfusion haemoglobin lower than before transfusion
Worsening anaemia and haemoglobinuria after each transfused unit
Reticulocytopenia in the face of severe anaemia
Rapid clinical deterioration in a patient with sickle cell disease
Signs of end-organ ischaemia from profound anaemia
reference.prognosis: The syndrome can be life-threatening, particularly if unrecognised and further transfusion is given, but it often responds to immunosuppression and avoidance of transfusion, with recovery of haemoglobin over days to weeks. Recurrence on re-exposure is a major concern, so future transfusion requires specialist planning.
pitfalls: Giving more blood in response to worsening anaemia and accelerating haemolysis.
Mistaking the presentation for a sickle cell painful crisis.
Assuming a negative antibody screen excludes the diagnosis, as the acute form may lack new antibodies.
Failing to start immunosuppression promptly in a deteriorating patient.
Not flagging the patient for specialist input before any future transfusion.
references: British Society for Haematology guidelines on the management of haemoglobinopathy transfusion
Mollison's Blood Transfusion in Clinical Medicine
management: Avoid further red-cell transfusion unless anaemia is immediately life-threatening, as additional units typically worsen the haemolysis
Start immunosuppression with corticosteroids and intravenous immunoglobulin as first-line therapy
Consider complement inhibition such as eculizumab and rituximab in severe or refractory cases
Support endogenous erythropoiesis with erythropoietin and provide folate and iron as appropriate while treating the underlying haemoglobinopathy
Monitor serial haemoglobin, lactate dehydrogenase, haptoglobin and reticulocyte count to track haemolysis and marrow recovery
If transfusion becomes unavoidable, use extended antigen-matched units in close liaison with the transfusion laboratory
Flag the diagnosis prominently to prevent inadvertent re-exposure and manage jointly with haematology and transfusion medicine
